entry.title: The new rules of cybersecurity
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The new rules of cybersecurityThe new rules of cybersecurity

Beyond compliance, regulations must prioritise speed and preparedness in responding to threats in the AI age

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Ajay TyagiBasu Chandola5 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 10:48 PM ISTIn July, AI agents undergoing cybersecurity evaluations at OpenAI circumvented restrictions on internet access and compromised systems belonging to Hugging Face, an external artificial intelligence (AI) platform. The incident highlighted an emerging cybersecurity challenge: Increasingly capable AI systems can identify and exploit vulnerabilities without direct human instructions.  As AI becomes integrated into critical digital infrastructure, these developments raise questions about the adequacy of existing cybersecurity frameworks. With AI enabling faster identification and exploitation of vulnerabilities, cybersecurity regulations must place greater emphasis on operational resilience.  AI is changing the cybersecurity ecosystem in two distinct ways. First, it can strengthen cybersecurity through vulnerability detection, network monitoring, and automated incident response, while enabling malicious actors to identify and exploit weaknesses more efficiently. Second, AI systems themselves introduce vulnerabilities. Techniques such as prompt injection can manipulate models through untrusted inputs, while autonomous agents can access external tools, databases, and operational systems. Weaknesses in the controls governing such access could have consequences beyond the AI application itself.  Recent advisories from India’s Computer Emergency Response Team (Cert-In) demonstrate the relevance of these concerns. In October, Cert-In reported incidents of AI agents undergoing evaluation accessing systems belonging to Indian organisations without authorisation. The affected organisations had not detected the intrusions themselves; the incidents were disclosed by AI model providers. Cert-In separately reported financially motivated campaigns involving agentic AI tools, where automation cut the time between initial compromise and impact from days to hours.  Another incident involving India’s digital certification provider eMudhra illustrates these challenges. On October 17, an independent researcher identified weak cryptographic keys associated with eight intermediate certificates, potentially using AI-assisted techniques, according to eMudhra. The vulnerabilities could have allowed attackers to issue fraudulent certificates and impersonate legitimate websites, prompting major browser providers to block the affected certificates. Significantly, the weaknesses had remained undetected despite independent audits.  These incidents highlight an important distinction. Many vulnerabilities remain conventional, including exposed credentials and inadequate access controls. However, AI can speed up their identification and exploitation, leaving organisations less time to respond. Cybersecurity approaches relying primarily on periodic audits, vulnerability assessments and scheduled remediation may, therefore, become insufficient.  India has an established cybersecurity architecture comprising legal, institutional and sector-specific mechanisms. The Information Technology Act, 2000, provides the legislative foundation, with Cert-In serving as the national agency for cybersecurity incident response and National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre responsible for protecting critical information infrastructure.   Cert-In’s directions also mandate reporting specified cybersecurity incidents within six hours, while the National Cyber Coordination Centre facilitates threat-intelligence sharing. These mechanisms are complemented by cybersecurity requirements introduced by sectoral regulators. The challenge is to ensure that this architecture remains effective against AI-related threats, particularly as attacks become faster and more sophisticated. Cert-In’s May 2026 blueprint recommends continuous vulnerability management, AI-aware monitoring and stronger incident-response capabilities. However, operational preparedness remains uneven. A 2025 study by the Data Security Council of India and Palo Alto Networks found that nearly 79 per cent of surveyed respondents planned to integrate AI into cybersecurity operations, while only around 8 per cent reported full integration.  India’s financial regulators offer examples of how cybersecurity principles can be translated into institutional responsibilities and measurable requirements. The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) directions on IT governance establish board-level responsibility for technology risks, information security, and business continuity. Its cybersecurity directions for non-bank payment system operators also address application security, third-party dependencies and incident response. The RBI’s FREE-AI Committee report adds recommendations for responsible AI adoption in finance.  The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) has adopted a more measurable approach. Its 2024 Cybersecurity and Cyber Resilience Framework introduced a Cyber Capability Index based on 23 weighted parameters, alongside periodic assessments for larger regulated entities. It provides for shared security operations centres to support smaller institutions. More recently, Sebi established a task force in response to advanced AI vulnerability-detection tools, to coordinate threat intelligence, vulnerability management and assessment of third-party risks. As AI changes the nature of cyber risks, the challenge is to adapt these arrangements rather than build a parallel regulatory system. Four priorities follow.  First, sectoral regulators should require cybersecurity assessments of AI systems deployed in critical sectors, both before deployment and following significant updates. These assessments should cover models, connected applications, credentials and agent permissions, including testing for unauthorised access and actions. Cert-In could develop common testing protocols, with independent evaluations for high-risk deployments.  Second, regulators should add measurable cyber resilience indicators to existing compliance requirements. Drawing on Sebi’s Cyber Capability Index, assessments could track the time taken to detect intrusions, contain compromised systems, revoke unauthorised access and restore critical services. These should be supported by regular simulation exercises and continuous vulnerability monitoring.  Third, Cert-In should establish a formal coordination mechanism with critical infrastructure authorities and sectoral regulators. This mechanism could develop common standards for classifying and reporting AI-related cybersecurity incidents, facilitate timely threat-intelligence sharing and coordinate responses to vulnerabilities affecting multiple organisations. Sectoral guidelines should also clarify the responsibilities of AI developers, deployers and third-party service providers, particularly where incidents arise from autonomous AI systems or shared technological infrastructure.  Fourth, India should prioritise operationalising the IndiaAI Safety Institute to strengthen cybersecurity testing and evaluation. The Institute could develop common standards for assessing vulnerabilities in AI models and autonomous agents, and establish shared testing facilities. These assessments could inform Cert-In and sectoral regulators in developing measurable requirements for AI-related cyber resilience.  India’s forthcoming consultation on AI regulation provides an opportunity to assess these issues.  The broader lesson is relevant beyond India. Existing cybersecurity regulations remain necessary, but their effectiveness will increasingly depend on how well they account for the changing speed and scale  of cyber threats. As AI becomes embedded in critical systems, cybersecurity governance must move beyond procedural compliance towards ensuring that institutions can anticipate, withstand, contain, and recover from emerging risks.

entry.title: When tariff walls become a ladder
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / When tariff walls become a ladderWhen tariff walls become a ladder

Tariffs, wars and global disorder are forging a more resilient India Inc

premium

Exporters are taking the shock on the chin, not treating trade friction as an impassable wall, but as a mirror reflecting the need for structural reform (Representative Image)

Sachchidanand Shukla5 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 10:58 PM ISTIndia is roughly 3 per cent of global gross domestic product (GDP) but nearly 20 per cent of its population. The arithmetic carries a hard truth: India’s next phase of growth cannot rely on the domestic market alone. It must win market share abroad by building businesses that can dominate internationally.  Paradoxically, Donald Trump’s trade offensive may, in fact, be helping. Corporate India is increasingly choosing grit over grievance. Exporters are taking the shock on the chin, not treating trade friction as an impassable wall, but as a mirror reflecting the need for structural reform. This baptism by trade fire is accelerating a long-overdue shift from cheap volume arbitrage towards complex manufacturing, scalar capabilities, research & development (R&D) and potentially towards proprietary brands.  The petroleum-refining sector that prompted US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to call India a “refining superpower” is a case in point. It illustrates resilience through scale, sophistication and market optionality. With capacity of roughly 258 million tonnes a year, and output capable of running above nameplate capacity, India imports crude, adds value through complex refining, and exports diesel, petrol, aviation fuel and naphtha to markets including the EU and even Russia. Redirecting cargoes while meeting domestic demand has strengthened energy security, foreign-exchange earnings and India’s ability to absorb geopolitical disruption.  Pharmaceuticals also show the stakes. Washington’s proposed framework — a phased duty of 100 per cent on imported generic medicines, escalating to 200 per cent  — strikes at the economics of an industry that sells 41 per cent of its generic-formulation exports to the US market. Yet, Indian drugmakers are not abandoning the world’s largest health care market. The tariff threat has made the shift from commodity generics to high-value innovation a corporate imperative.  Sun Pharma’s $11.8-billion acquisition of Organon; Lupin’s commitment of $250 million in Florida to local manufacturing and R&D are recent examples. Of about $20.5 billion in US investment pledges announced by Indian leaders at the SelectUSA summit, $19 billion came from pharma. The model is moving from exporting to onshore, high-value manufacturing and speciality drugs.  Clean energy tells a similar story. When the US imposed a preliminary 126 per cent countervailing duty on Indian solar-cell imports, the companies did not shrink capacity. They redirected volumes towards Europe and West Asia, while using the production-linked incentive scheme to move into high-efficiency modules. Rather than remain dependent on raw cell exports, firms are climbing the supply chain through module assembly and local manufacturing abroad.  In the second quarter of 2026-27, export performance reinforces the broader point. Merchandise exports rose 18 per cent year-on-year (YoY) to $260 billion, one of the fastest increases since 2023, while goods-and-services exports increased 14 per cent to $476 billion. Petroleum-product exports rose 32 per cent YoY in September, keeping up its stellar growth rate through first half of the year. True, there is an element of higher prices accounting for a bulk of this growth, as against volume increase. Total exports expanded from $498 billion in FY21 to a record $863 billion in FY26, with a significant pivot from agricultural commodities, gems and textiles towards technology-intensive production and specialised services.  Importantly, the export basket now looks materially different. Electronics that clocked 70 per cent YoY growth in September rose from $11 billion in FY21 to $48 billion in FY26, lifting its share in merchandise exports from a low single-digit to 10.8 per cent. Engineering goods exceed 26 per cent of shipments, helping push non-petroleum exports to $388 billion.  The $421-billion services sector is moving beyond routine IT support into consulting, finance and engineering design. Threats of border taxes on cross-border data flows and tightening visa rules are dismantling the legacy business model of cheap headcount arbitrage. The industry heavyweights are transforming offshore delivery centres into specialised hubs dedicated to enterprise AI, Cloud architecture, and cybersecurity, embedding themselves deeply into global corporate infrastructures.   To hedge against single-market regulatory shocks, tech giants are simultaneously expanding nearshore delivery networks across Latam and Eastern Europe. EU exports reached $86 billion, with deeper reach into France, Italy and the Czech Republic. New corridors across West Africa and Southern Africa are carrying pharmaceuticals, automobiles and industrial machinery. Trade deals, commercial diplomacy and China+1 realignments are reinforcing this shift. Agreements with the EU, the UK, Australia, New Zealand and Oman widen preferential access for goods and open channels for services.  But tariffs do not automatically create competitiveness. They can destroy margins, displace workers and expose weak balance sheets. India must use external pressure to accelerate reforms it needed anyway — namely, lower logistics costs, predictable regulation, reliable infrastructure, deeper skills and patient capital.  The American tariff offensive was meant to assert leverage and pull supply chains home. It is instead hastening the growth and industrial evolution of America’s most consequential democratic global partner. For India, doubling from 3 per cent of global GDP and ultimately to 10 per cent, will require more than merely exporting more; it will require creating capabilities and franchises the world cannot easily replace.  Indian enterprise should trade volume for value — and policymakers must sustain a diversified, multipolar trade architecture. The ultimate irony will then be clear: Protectionism intended as a wall will have become a ladder, lifting a more resilient India, even if belatedly, towards the centre of global commerce.       
The writer is group chief economist, L&T. The views are personal     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. They do not necessarily reflect the opinion of www.business-standard.com or the Business Standard newspaperTopics : BS Opinion Indian exports Global Trade US tariffs

entry.title: Risk of irrelevance?
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Risk of irrelevance?Risk of irrelevance?

The scale of the selling and the speed and magnitude of the underperformance in Indian equities are unsustainable

premium

Foreign portfolio investors have withdrawn $65 billion from Indian equities since September 2024, amid sharp market underperformance and declining global investor interest. | Illustration: Binay Sinha

Akash Prakash6 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 12:19 AM ISTI have been investing in Indian equities for over 30 years. Rarely have I seen foreign sentiment this bad. India no longer features in global conversations. What I am saying is not new. Since the Indian market’s peak in September 2024, we have seen $65 billion in net outflows by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs). Over the last decade, India has received zero net-foreign flows.  The stock of Indian equities owned by foreigners has fallen from $930 billion to about $675 billion, and foreign ownership as a percentage of the market is now at a 15-year low. India is now a consensus underweight for all global investors and our weighting itself has shrunk from 21 per cent in September 2024 to about 10 per cent today (MSCI Emerging Market index).  One company, TSMC, has a benchmark weight 50 per cent higher than that of all of India! The three EM heavyweights — TSMC, Samsung Electronics, and SK Hynix — together account for 30 per cent of the index, but have almost three times India’s weighting.  We have also seen unprecedented underperformance. Since the peak in September 2024, Indian equities are down about 25 per cent in dollar terms, even as the EM indices are up about 50 per cent. We have, therefore, underperformed by 7,500 basis points (75 percentage points) in the last two years alone. I have never in my career seen this quantum of underperformance in this short a period. It has destroyed careers and blown up funds. There are numerous funds that have destroyed 10-year track records in the last 24 months by simply being overweight India.  Normally, I would look at these statistics and numbers as contrarian indicators. This is exactly why I would argue — and still do — that we will soon see a turnaround in India’s relative and absolute performance. The scale of the selling and the speed and magnitude of the underperformance are unsustainable. How can three companies in Asia have three times the index weight of a country with India’s size and potential?  How can these three companies have a combined index weight of 30 per cent, almost identical to the combined weight of India and China, at 30.5 per cent? Something is clearly wrong. It seems ludicrous that three Asian technology companies can have an index weight almost equivalent to 40 per cent of the world’s population. A classic contrarian indicator, if there ever was one.  However, what troubles me is that for the first time I am now being asked about the need for an India-dedicated allocation. Many allocators no longer think India is important enough to warrant dedicated exposure. Why bother with sticking their neck out and betting on India specifically, especially given the extent of underperformance. This conversation has come up now after years. Twenty years ago, every allocator had dedicated money in China and Brazil, and India was a debate. Over time, it became conventional wisdom that to invest in EM, you needed dedicated pools of capital for India, greater China and Brazil. If allocators are now unwilling to make an India-specific bet, it is a big negative and will constrain the quantum of foreign equity as well as the diversity of capital into the country. Non-dedicated exposure by definition is more cyclical.  So why this change in thinking? First of all, it is the decline in India’s EM weighting. At only 10 per cent, we are half what we used to be and three countries — Taiwan, Korea and China — are 70 per cent of the EM index. Do you really need to bother with India? Even getting India wrong will not really move the needle. Over the last 10 years, India has anyway underperformed the EM indices by about 180 basis points annually. Even on a 20-year basis, India has just marginally outperformed. The narrative that you need to be in India because of the quality of companies, sustainability of growth and entrepreneurial energy is getting lost. There is fundamentally less belief that we have decades of strong growth ahead of us.  Second, many investors have come to the conclusion that India may not deliver enough absolute returns. Their calculations are as follows. The Nifty index in rupees has delivered about 10.5 per cent per annum over the last 20 years. Assuming a capital gains tax impact of about 15 per cent (the average of the short-term rate of 20 per cent and the long-term rate of 12.5 per cent), this brings the return down to about 8.9 per cent. Then, assuming a near 4 per cent rupee depreciation (the average over the last 20 years), this brings the return down to about 6 per cent in dollar terms.  Why bother with 6 per cent when the 100-year annualised returns in US equities are about 10 per cent? I would argue that 25-year Nifty returns are near 13.5 per cent not 10 per cent. Nifty returns understate market returns and assuming continued 4 per cent currency depreciation makes no sense given the narrowing inflation differentials. Also, given the valuations, can you assume continued 10 per cent compounding in the United States? However, it does not matter what I think, this is what investors are saying.  All allocators are upset about the capital gains tax. They do not pay these taxes in any other major jurisdiction. It drops projected long-term annualised returns by about 2 per cent and that is a huge difference when comparing countries over long holding periods. There is also the perception that India remains a complex place to do business. Indian service providers do a good job of scaring the risk and compliance teams of global investors. While this may be unfair, the perception sticks.  India is also seen as the biggest global loser from artificial intelligence (AI), as our key advantages of demographics and a skilled white-collar workforce lose relevance in an AI-first world. Innovation and research & development, which are driving value creation globally, are seen as areas of weakness in India. One can refute this argument, but many allocators believe it.  India is also caught in a no-man’s land, not cheap enough for value investors to pile in but not growing fast enough to attract growth investors either.  If India were to lose its attraction as an independent asset class that is a cause of worry. We will attract less structural capital and be of less relevance to global allocators. Not a good place to be for a country fundamentally short of capital. Equity markets are a competitive advantage for India, we weaken this if we lose access to dedicated pools of long-term capital.  I remain convinced that all this data is more a contrarian indicator and not a reason to turn more negative on India. Much of this is cyclical and the tide will turn. However, we must guard against slipping further down the investor consideration set in the meantime.  
           The writer is with Amansa Capital   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Advance Authorisation: Job work abroad and its key tax implications
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Advance Authorisation: Job work abroad and its key tax implicationsAdvance Authorisation: Job work abroad and its key tax implications

Experts clarify rules on overseas job work under advance authorisation, leasing capital goods under EPCG and timelines for invoicing and export shipments

premium

Exporters must comply with customs and GST rules for overseas job work and shipments (Representative Image)

TNC Rajagopalan3 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 12:05 AM ISTWe have an export order for an item. We have imported the materials required for manufacturing the item duty free under an advance authorisation. One of our machines to carry out a specialised process has broken down. It will take quite some time to send the machine abroad for repairs and get it back. Our customer cannot wait that long. So, we want to send the imported duty-free material abroad to get the specialised process done and re-import it for further manufacture at our factory. We refer to Paragraph 4.33 of the Handbook of Procedures (HBP), which allows the endorsement of the name of the supporting manufacturer in an advance authorisation. Can we get endorsement of the name of a supporting manufacturer abroad and if so, what are the tax implications?  Para 4.33 of the HBP does not expressly restrict endorsement only to supporting manufacturers or job workers located in India. You can therefore seek endorsement of the overseas job worker’s name and address, explaining that the materials will return to India for further manufacture and subsequent export towards discharge of the export obligation. The proviso to condition (xii) of notification number 21/2023-Customs permits transfer of imported materials for job work subject to the relevant GST (Goods and Services Tax) conditions. Those provisions do not expressly prohibit overseas job work. You should comply with the applicable job-work-challan, recordkeeping, reporting and return-period requirements, and declare the purpose of the temporary export in the shipping bill. On re-import, the processed goods will attract duty under Section 20 of the Customs Act, 1962, read with any applicable exemption notification. The original duty-free import under the Advance Authorisation does not necessarily exempt this re-import. The invoice of the foreign job-worker will not attract IGST on reverse charge basis because where the specialized process is performed entirely abroad on goods physically made available to the foreign job worker, the place of supply is outside the taxable territory in accordance with Section 13(3)(a) of the IGST Act, 2017.  In the previous Foreign Trade Policy (FTP), capital goods could be imported under Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG) even if the same were financed by a leasing company. In the current FTP 2023, there is no such provision. Can we import capital goods on lease basis and clear under EPCG scheme even in current policy 2023?  Para 2.33 of the FTP permits import of capital goods under lease financing without specific DGFT permission. Also, the current definition of ‘importer’ in the Customs Act, 1962 covers the lessee even for import under the EPCG scheme.  Our customer wants us to raise the invoice but delay export shipment by two months. Can we do that?  Yes. Section 31(1) of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017 requires you to raise the invoice before or at the time of removal. However, Rule 96A of the CGST Rules, 2017 requires you to export the goods removed under Letter of Undertaking or bond within three months from the date of invoice (not removal from the factory). The Commissioner may extend the period.

entry.title: Uneasy lies the governance space
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Uneasy lies the governance spaceUneasy lies the governance space

The ripples the Tata affair will cause are yet to become clear - but promoters will be nervous at such a coup by the professional hire

premium

The governance tensions at Tata Sons have raised questions about promoter control, board independence and the balance of power between shareholders and professional management. | Photo: File

Rama Bijapurkar5 min read Last Updated : Oct 26 2026 | 10:05 PM ISTL’affaire Tata Sons has brought into focus the uneasy space between promoters, professional managers, and boards, that India Inc constantly negotiates. While there has not been much public comment from India Inc on the situation (and this columnist rushes in where angels fear to tread), there has been enormous private speculation about how this situation came to pass, and nervous conjecture on what the ripple effects of this will be in shaping the future governance space.   This is neither a spat among shareholder groups for control, nor a summary sacking of a chief executive officer by a promoter. We have seen those movies before. This is almost the first time that a professional manager-CEO, with the board on his side and non-shareholder government institutions weighing in, has sought to marginalise a 66 per cent-owning promoter in decision choices that impact not just the direction of the business (though we are not explicitly hearing from either side about strategic fault lines), but also the promoter’s shareholding.   While CEOs pushing back publicly and openly fighting shareholders is common in bastions of capitalism like the United States, with widely distributed shareholding and boards playing a greater fiduciary role, in India such battles are rare, especially if it is a promoter shareholder. Indian promoters hold the hallowed place of a company’s birth parents with special rights and responsibilities — some enshrined in law, others in culture.   ITC and Larsen & Toubro (L&T) are two unforgettable examples in India of CEO-shareholder battles. In the case of ITC, the battle was against promoter BAT’s  (British American Tobacco’s) move to gain control of the company and stop diversification, while in the case of L&T, it was against a dominant shareholder group, with the CEO fighting to retain management control. In both cases, the government backed the CEO, but by weighing in through its 30 to 40 per cent shareholding via financial institutions it controlled, keeping within the legitimate norm of capitalism: Jiski lathi, uski bhains (whoever has the stick owns the buffalo).   What makes the present Tata Sons case different is that government-controlled entities do not own large chunks of shares, and the duelling ground is not an annual general meeting or extraordinary general meeting. That a CEO with no shareholding backing, along with board members who do not represent chunks of shareholding, can challenge a promoter with a 66 per cent holding and pressure it to dilute its stake, and not have sway over decisions is a first-time challenge to power structures — which have stood the test of time, tradition, convention, and culture, rightly or wrongly. It brings a fresh round of calibration, especially by promoters, of their terms of endearment and engagement with professional CEOs, not to mention boards. More so, if their shareholding is well below 51 per cent.  The relationship between professional managers and promoters in India has always had a degree of tension. The differences that typically end in the CEO quitting could be on several dimensions —differences in direction, risk appetite and prudence, business ambition, remuneration (less so of late as CEO salaries and stock options have zoomed upwards) and often over different perceptions of where the power to make what kind of decisions rests — the birth parent or the foster parent. Human resources consultants frequently counsel boards and CEOs that once the chemistry with the promoter has gone sour, there is no salvaging the relationship.   The separation of management from ownership is not common in India yet, though nascent examples are emerging. Big stock market influencers welcome owner presence in management because they feel a reassuring common focus on increasing shareholder value.  Many employees also prefer a promoter at the helm, seeing this as offering more predictability and benevolence than the CEO or the board of the day. Even in a company like Infosys,  set up by professionals, the “founders” (as they preferred to be called) took turns in running the company in accordance with their pre-agreed plan. The board went along with the frequent changes at the top, presumably because these were the promoters who had built an amazing company and it seemed only fair that they each had their turn.   Given the promoter-friendly, promoter-respectful and promoter-on-top ethos of corporate governance that has existed and continues to exist in India, this departure from the norm against none other than the venerated, iconic Tata promoter group with its track record of trusteeship and larger good over personal gain has rocked the comfort boat all around.  The ripples it will cause are yet to become clear — will promoters be nervous seeing such a coup by the professional hire? How will they respond? Will they pick boards like in the old days, based on loyalty and narrow subject-matter expertise? Especially as the law of the land and the market regulator push more power and accountability in the hands of independent directors? Will boards be now placed under more pressure from external directives on which way to vote, getting trapped between the rock and the hard place of the promoter and the proverbial hand of God? Will CEOs have less freedom to operate and more fetters? And does this add to the bad rap that India has been getting of late as a safe, stable place to invest in for the long term? Probably yes to all.  Since one big pillar of the argument is the national and systemic importance of Tata Sons, its board perhaps needs to be more transparent on the rationale for its many volte-faces.

entry.title: Return of SEZ goods: Welcome relief, unresolved issues
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Return of SEZ goods: Welcome relief, unresolved issuesReturn of SEZ goods: Welcome relief, unresolved issues

The government's new SEZ rules allow customs duty refunds on goods returned after failed deliveries, but a short deadline and unresolved drawback disputes leave gaps for domestic buyers and exporters

premium

Goods returned from Special Economic Zones to the domestic market may qualify for customs duty refunds under the amended rules

TNC Rajagopalan3 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 11:44 PM ISTThe government has amended Rule 49(2) of the Special Economic Zones (SEZ) Rules, 2006, providing for refund of Customs duty when domestic tariff area (DTA) buyers return duty-paid goods to SEZ units following failure to  take delivery. The relief is  welcome but restrictive and leaves unresolved disputes over drawback claims relating to earlier returns.  The notification dated October 15, 2026, covers cases where a DTA buyer fails to take delivery because of changes in fashion, market conditions or default in conditions of the sale agreement. The goods must return within thirty days of clearance. The DTA buyer who paid or bore the duty can claim refund under Section 27 of the Customs Act, 1962. The goods must be identified to the satisfaction of the specified officer and evidence furnished that the DTA buyer has not availed any benefits, including input tax credit (ITC). The SEZ unit must furnish that evidence and maintain a separate auditable inventory of returned goods. The amendment permits SEZ units to resell returned goods in their original condition to the same or another DTA buyer, on payment of applicable duties as a fresh sale. The repair facility is retained.  Previously, Rule 49(2) allowed return of goods supplied by SEZ units only for repairs. It contained no express provision for refund on failed deliveries. The new provision addresses a practical difficulty faced by domestic buyers and SEZ suppliers. However, thirty days from clearance is a short period for resolving a failed delivery and arranging return. There is no express provision for extending the deadline. More importantly, the wording covers a buyer who fails to take delivery, leaving doubt about goods rejected after delivery. The explanation below S.No.15 of Annexure-I to notification 52/2003-Cus dated March 31, 2003, relating to export-oriented units (EOUs) clarifies that failure of the foreign buyer to take delivery includes rejection of goods by that buyer. A similar explanation should be inserted now to cover rejection by DTA buyers. The requirement that no benefits should have been availed also leaves unclear whether ITC initially taken but subsequently reversed will suffice. This too needs clarification.  The amendment operates prospectively. Earlier, DTA buyers filed drawback bills of export under Section 74 of the Customs Act when returning identifiable, duty-paid goods to SEZ units. Customs disputed some claims because the definition of export under the Customs Act and the 1995 Re-export Drawback Rules did not include DTA supplies to SEZs. CBIC Instruction No.06/2026-Customs, dated April 27, 2026, recognised SEZ clearances into DTA as imports for Section 74 drawback purposes. However, it did not expressly address whether sending goods from DTA to SEZ qualifies as export for that section. This issue affects both returns of goods procured from SEZs and supplies of goods originally imported from abroad. The controversy persists despite Section 2(m)(ii) of the SEZ Act, 2005, recognising DTA supplies to SEZ units for authorised operations as exports, and Section 51 giving that Act overriding effect where other laws are inconsistent.  The government should allow more time for returns, empower authorities to extend the deadline, and provide refund of duty for goods returned for any reason, with safeguards. It should clarify that Section 74 drawback is available on duty-paid imported goods sent to SEZs. Prospective relief should be accompanied by resolution of past disputes on the same issue.

entry.title: Market reforms: The unfinished agenda
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Market reforms: The unfinished agendaMarket reforms: The unfinished agenda

Consistent publication of dispute rulings, standardised document requirements for claims and a name-based search facility could help families trace unclaimed mutual fund investments

premium

Harsh Roongta4 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 11:05 PM ISTRatan, a friend, was buying his dream home. The seller had brought the registration forward by a day, and his mutual fund redemption money was now due on that very day. He needed it in the morning to get a pay order for the afternoon appointment. His question was simple. At what time would the money reach his bank account? By 8 am, it had. What struck me was that his worry had been about the hour. He had taken the date for granted.  Anyone who invested in shares a few decades ago will understand why Ratan’s confidence struck me. Payments could be delayed, and physical share transfers could get stuck for months over signature mismatches. Today, trades settle the next working day and shares arrive directly in your demat account. With the UPI block facility, your money can stay in your bank account earning interest until needed for a purchase. Scams and payment crises prompted many of these changes, often after investors had paid dearly. Each reform meant changing practices that somebody benefited from.  The confidence these reforms have helped build is particularly visible in mutual funds. Entry loads, deducted from your money before it was even invested, were abolished in 2009. Direct plans followed in 2013, allowing investors to avoid distributor commissions. Clearer scheme categories made funds easier to understand and compare, while the riskometer showed how risky each scheme is. Investors now put over ₹32,000 crore every month through systematic investment plans (SIPs), with investments held through SIPs worth nearly ₹18 lakh crore. This confidence was built while openly acknowledging the risks. Advertisements repeatedly reminded investors that mutual fund investments are subject to market risk and returns are not guaranteed.  The improvements extend to families claiming investments after a death. Your family can now report the death to a single intermediary, and the other intermediaries must contact the nominee with the procedure and documents required. We saw this work smoothly when a deceased client’s family received his mutual funds and shares within 10 days of submitting documents.   But families can still face unreasonable demands where there is no nominee or surviving joint holder. While claiming my late father’s unclaimed shares, I was asked for my mother’s death certificate from 1963. Families need predictable document requirements in every case.  An arbitrator on the Securities and Exchange Board of India’s (Sebi’s) Online Dispute Resolution (SMART ODR) platform ruled in my favour on that demand. But why should the next investor have to fight the same battle? Publishing decisions with personal details removed would help investors understand their rights and discourage intermediaries from repeating unreasonable demands. Sebi already requires this publication, but it is not done consistently. And if analysis shows the same complaint recurring, the cause should be fixed rather than each case fought one by one.   Then there is money that families have lost track of. Unclaimed mutual fund dividends and redemption proceeds were ₹3,811 crore as on March 31, 2026. MITRA (Mutual Fund Investment Tracing and Retrieval Assistant) helps trace inactive folios, but only if you have the investment details. How can the children provide those details when they do not even know whether the parent invested in mutual funds? The Investor Education and Protection Fund (IEPF) allows a search for unclaimed shares by name. A similar search across mutual funds would let children start with a parent’s name and discover whether anything is lying unclaimed. The usual worry is fraud. But entitlement is checked before payment, so fraud by a few should not stop families from claiming what is rightfully theirs.   Truth be told, the confidence Ratan has was built one reform at a time. The remaining gaps can be closed the same way, and none needs new technology or a new law. Sebi can ensure that ODR decisions are published, as its own rules already require. It can lay down one complete list of documents for claims, beyond which nothing may be asked. And it can allow a name search for unclaimed mutual fund money, as IEPF already does for shares. Ratan worried only about the hour. Every investor deserves the same confidence.

entry.title: The neglected species of pulses
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The neglected species of pulsesThe neglected species of pulses

Reviving neglected pulses could boost nutrition, reduce imports and improve farmers' incomes

premium

Underutilised pulses could strengthen India’s nutritional security while supporting farmers and reducing import dependence

Surinder Sud5 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 10:46 PM ISTIn a country where pulses (dal) are the major source of protein for most people, malnutrition is rampant, and import dependence for meeting pulses requirements is substantial, the suboptimal utilisation of the existing diversity of indigenous legumes is hard to justify. Only eight of the available 14 species of pulses are grown and consumed on a regular basis. The others (leguminous crops) have either been abandoned or are cultivated and consumed in specific areas on a small scale. Many of these underexploited species have impressive nutritional profiles. Their mainstreaming can be a boon to consumers, as also to small and marginal farmers, who have traditionally been growing these hardy and drought-resistant crops in arid, semi-arid, and degraded lands, but have stopped doing so because of waning market demand.  These underutilised species include Moth bean (Moth dal), Lathyrus (Khesari dal), Horse gram (Kulthi), Faba bean (Bakla or Kala matar), Rice bean (Sutri or Lal bean), and Adzuki bean (Lal mung or Lal chowri). Their farming is confined to limited areas, chiefly for local consumption. Going by their merits, in terms of versatility, ease of cultivation, and health benefits, these deserve better usage.  Unfortunately, these species of pulses have been neglected even by agricultural scientists and are, therefore, often dubbed as “orphan crops”. Not enough research & development has been done to improve their productivity, grain quality, processability, and marketability by developing superior high-yielding crop strains. Such apathy towards these valuable legumes is unwarranted, given the dire need to augment the availability of protein-dense foods to strengthen nutritional security.  The country’s pulses sector is dominated by just five legumes, which together account for 90 per cent of production and consumption. These are pigeon pea (tur or arhar), chickpea (chana or gram), green gram (mung), black gram (urad), and lentil (masoor). The bulk of the remaining 10 per cent consumption is shared by three pulses – red kidney beans (Rajma), black eyed peas (Lobiya), and field peas (Matar).  There are, indeed, several good reasons for harnessing the untapped potential of the little-used pulses. For one, these can boost the domestic supply of legumes to reduce pulses imports, which amounted to 7 million tonnes in 2024-25 and 6 million tonnes in 2025-26. Besides, these pulses can grow on poor-quality lands not ideally suited for cultivating main cereals and commercial crops. In fact, being leguminous crops, these can improve the fertility of such lands by fixing atmospheric nitrogen in the soil. These crops can, therefore, serve virtually as an effective means of regenerating degraded lands, which abound in India, spanning over 98 million hectares. Moreover, these crops, requiring little investment in cash inputs, can be a vital livelihood support for resource-starved farmers owning such lands. And most importantly, they are regarded by farm scientists as a repository of genes that might prove useful in imparting climate change-resilience, immunity against diseases and pests, and other desirable traits, in future crop species.  Interestingly, most of these underexploited crops possess significant amounts of dietary fibre and bioactive compounds, which can mitigate the challenges posed by the rising incidence of lifestyle and flawed nutrition-induced ailments, such as diabetes, hypertension, obesity, cardiovascular diseases, and even cancer.  The reasons for these species of pulses falling out of favour, though formidable, are not difficult to overcome. Many of their drawbacks can be remedied through simple treatment and managerial intervention, such as soaking in water or processing them into value-added products to prepare nutritious snacks. In the case of Moth bean, for instance, the main problem is the long time it takes to cook. This can easily be cut down to half by soaking the grains in water overnight. Preparing in a pressure cooker can reduce it further.  The Khesari dal, which has a very high protein content of 26-28 per cent, was temporarily banned because of the rise in the incidence of neurological disorder called lathyrism (paralysis of lower limbs) among its regular consumers in regions like Bihar, Jharkhand and eastern Uttar Pradesh. Scientific studies later revealed that this condition was caused due to the presence of a neurotoxin, called beta-ODAP, in Khesari dal, and affected primarily those who ate this cheapest available legume almost as a staple. Studies also showed that the problem could be largely solved by soaking it in salt water, and discarding the water. This lowers the toxin level down to almost safe limits, especially if consumed in moderation.  Sprouting is another simple and effective way of improving the digestibility of these less used pulses, and also their acceptability among people. It activates their internal enzymes, which transform these grains into nutritional powerhouses.  There is, thus, a strong case for making better use of the underexploited legumes to enhance the overall availability of pulses. The Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses, set up last year to make the country self-sufficient in pulses by 2030-31, would hopefully do the needful in this direction.

entry.title: Can your refrigerator be hacked?
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Can your refrigerator be hacked?Can your refrigerator be hacked?

Consumers and corporations will have to be as careful about protecting appliances as they are with office equipment, like computers and servers

premium

Any connected device deserves enterprise-level cybersecurity protocols | Representative Picture

Pranjal Sharma4 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 10:44 PM ISTBeing smart can be a weakness, especially for everyday appliances that are part of daily lives. As machines, appliances and devices get more connected, they provide increasing ease of use.   Smart appliances such as refrigerators, ovens, microwaves, dishwashers, washing machines, and air conditioners are no longer just standalone household devices. They are increasingly connected to the internet, mobile apps, sensors, and artificial intelligence (AI) systems to improve convenience, energy efficiency, safety, and food management.  A smart refrigerator can monitor internal temperatures, alert users if the door is left open, track inventory through cameras or barcode scanning, and suggest recipes based on available ingredients. Some advanced models from companies such as Samsung and LG can synchronise with grocery shopping apps, create shopping lists, and even automatically reorder frequently used products.  However, this connectivity can be weaponised to convert the appliances into devices of destruction. Appliances placed in homes, restaurants, offices, industrial sites and government buildings are no longer harmless tools of convenience. Connected household appliances such as smart refrigerators, microwaves, ovens, televisions, cameras, and thermostats have become increasingly attractive targets for cybercriminals, because they often have internet connectivity, but weaker security controls than traditional computers. Security experts have repeatedly demonstrated that these devices can be compromised and used as entry points into broader home or enterprise networks.  An early case occurred in 2014, when researchers discovered a botnet composed of internet-connected devices, including smart refrigerators and televisions, that had been hijacked to send hundreds of thousands of spam emails. The recent hacking of fridges of supermarket chains in France has revived fears of hacked appliances.   French supermarket chains, including Intermarché, E.Leclerc, and Système U lost millions worth of frozen food, after attackers gained access to refrigeration management systems and remotely altered temperature settings.   The attackers targeted refrigeration control technology, changing settings so that refrigeration units continuously defrosted and temperatures reportedly rose as high as 50°C, effectively turning cooling systems into heaters.  Many more unnoticed hacks are occurring across millions of connected devices. Industry data indicates that the threat environment is worsening. Research from Bitdefender and NETGEAR found that the average connected household experienced approximately 29 cyberattacks per day in 2025, with attacks increasingly targeting consumer electronics such as smart TVs, streaming devices, cameras, and other connected appliances. The study observed billions of attack attempts across millions of households, highlighting how smart home devices have become routine targets for automated cybercriminal activity. Smart appliances can enable indirect surveillance. A connected refrigerator, thermostat, smart lighting system, or washing machine may reveal occupancy patterns, sleep schedules, vacation periods, or daily routines through usage logs. Even without accessing cameras or microphones, an attacker who obtains this data may be able to determine when people are home, asleep, or away.  Connected appliances placed in commercial locations and government offices can be used for spying and gathering data. Connected building controls, refrigeration systems, industrial sensors, and surveillance devices can provide information about operating schedules, facility utilisation, inventory levels, and employee activity. Smart speakers represent another potential hacking concern. While devices such as Amazon Echo, Google Nest, and Apple HomePod are designed to activate only after hearing a wake word, security researchers have demonstrated techniques that can manipulate voice assistants or exploit software vulnerabilities to gather information or trigger actions. More commonly, privacy concerns arise from the amount of voice and behavioral data stored in cloud systems, rather than from direct hacking.  Consumers and corporations will have to be as careful about protecting appliances as they are with office equipment, like computers and servers. If a smart appliance is connected to the same router as the enterprise, it offers a vulnerable entry point for hacking the entire system. Hacking a fridge in an inhouse café of a large corporation can be as risky as hacking a laptop or a mobile device. Any connected device, from a wrist watch to a washing machine, deserves enterprise level cyber security protocols.    Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: A stunning turnaround
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / A stunning turnaroundA stunning turnaround

Lula da Silva has multiple challenges

premium

Brazil President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva(Photo:PTI)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 10:34 PM ISTThe re-election of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva as President of Brazil has come as a shock to both markets and his domestic Opposition. His challenger, Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of the controversial former President, Jair Bolsonaro, had taken a handy lead in the first round of the presidential elections. This led, perhaps, to a certain degree of overconfidence among the right-wing challengers. In the end, thanks to an enormous effort to increase the turnout, the incumbent President pulled through a second-round victory, which didn’t appear close. This has never happened in Brazil’s history. For Mr Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, this election will no doubt be his last. But it will cement his reputation as South America’s most influential democratic left-wing politician of the past century. His story, from his beginning as a metal-worker, to his time in the trade unions, to victories in presidential elections, will inspire left-wingers across the continent, especially because much of the rest of it is dominated by the right.  President Lula’s last election was marred by what amounted to an abortive coup attempt launched by Jair Bolsonaro’s allies. Fortunately, there appears to be no such effort in progress on this occasion. The challenges for Mr Lula this time will be external. It is not his domestic Opposition but global markets that will revolt. And United States President Donald Trump has made no secret of his sympathy for Mr Bolsonaro, and has already declared that the election to him “looked rigged”. Of these two adversaries, the markets are the more concerning at present. Flavio Bolsonaro, in the course of his campaign, stressed the poor macroeconomic situation that Brazil was in. The numbers are, indeed, worrying. In the four years since Jair Bolsonaro was ousted in 2022, the country’s debt-to-gross domestic product ratio has increased from about 72 per cent to about 83 per cent. High interest costs and the left’s spending commitments make debt servicing quite hard; and there is no credible path towards consolidation that Mr Lula has laid out.  Unsurprisingly, the surprise news that he had been re-elected caused markets to fall. The stock market fell almost 14 per cent in one day, hitting the circuit breaker. Brazil’s currency, the real, fell more than 8 per cent against the dollar, its sharpest one-day drop since 2002. Real-denominated 10-year bond yields rose by more than 2 percentage points, hitting around 15 per cent. All of this deeply complicates Mr Lula’s attempts at stabilisation. He will not want to cut spending or benefits, and indeed plans to increase the wages (and thereby affect the path of future pensions, worsening the fiscal situation). But he cannot raise taxes easily to compensate because his party does not control the legislature, which has repeatedly resisted any attempt to raise the effective tax rate by closing loopholes.  It is likely, therefore, that if Mr Lula wants to work on his legacy over this term, he will look to geopolitics rather than economics. He may well take on the position of primary resister to the new Monroe doctrine that has been espoused by Mr Trump’s second administration. If so, India should expect a Brazil even more committed to counter-mobilisation against the US, and old-style “third-worldism”, than before.     Topics : Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment Brazil Elections Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva

entry.title: Ethanol in the fast lane
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Ethanol in the fast laneEthanol in the fast lane

A slower transition can address unanticipated impacts

premium

The fact that ethanol distilleries tend to be located close to agri-hubs also plays a role in creating employment opportunities and promotes some measure of rural development

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 10:27 PM ISTThe Ministry of Road Transport and Highways’ decision to allow E100 and E85 fuels, along with the registration of flex-fuel vehicles, is understandable in the light of the geopolitical outlook on oil prices in the foreseeable future and growing urban pollution, much of which is transport-related. But the wisdom of such policy speed may need to be balanced with the anticipated negative externalities associated with the ethanol journey. Already, the mandated shift to E20 from E10 five years ahead of the original schedule, prompted no doubt by prolonged supply constraints and the need to meet “Net Zero” targets, has annoyed car owners, who have reported a 7-12 per cent drop in fuel efficiency, which somewhat negates the argument of lowering fuel demand. According to the government data, however, the country has saved ₹1.9 trillion in imports of crude oil and substituted 31 million tonnes between April, when the E20 mandate came into force, and mid-October, though some analysts have questioned the arithmetic behind these calculations.  On the face of it, the drive towards an ethanol-powered automotive future has been a win-win. It has reportedly helped stabilise farm incomes, especially in Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka, by offering a predictable market for agri-surpluses and also absorbing damaged foodgrain from the system. The fact that ethanol distilleries tend to be located close to agri-hubs also plays a role in creating employment opportunities and promotes some measure of rural development. But the long-term impacts on food security and ecology remain open questions. The impact was evident in the sugar market earlier this year, when low opening stocks and production resulted in a sharp rise in sugar prices. Meanwhile, the government has rebutted the accusation of larger diversions of the rice stocks, underlining that Food Corporation of India, the government procurement agency, only diverted damaged or broken grain for ethanol production and did not endanger the food-security programme.  But over time and given the uncertainties of agri-markets, the rapid expansion of the ethanol programme could well incentivise farmers to divert larger tracts of land towards sugar or maize cultivation, which raises a fresh set of problems. This is exemplified by Brazil, which is regarded as a global success story in the ethanol transition. The 25-year transition, which started in 1975, has undoubtedly helped bring about  a sharp reduction in greenhouse-gas emission but has had a deleterious effect on local ecology. As farmers there started converting more and more arable land for maize and sugarcane, they displaced livestock and cattle ranchers, who then simply cleared large tracts of the Amazon rainforest to expand. The country also faced occasional price and supply asymmetries; when global prices of sugar rose, supplies available for the ethanol programme inevitably fell. Equally, the sugar crop was diverted to ethanol producers when ethanol prices rose.  In India, there is also the question of whether promoting water-intensive crops like sugarcane on a large scale for the ethanol programme is warranted when agri-inputs — fertiliser, water, and electricity — are either heavily subsidised or free. On balance, given the complexities of India’s agricultural policies, it may be better to move more gradually on the ethanol transition rather than steer abruptly into the fast lane.     Topics : Ethanol blending Fuel ethanol Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Pricing pain points
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Pricing pain pointsPricing pain points

Controls in health care are needed but come with risks

premium

The government has acknowledged steep hospital markups on medicines and medical consumables, raising concerns over healthcare affordability and the need for stronger pricing regulations. (Photo: Shutterstock)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 26 2026 | 10:10 PM ISTThe government’s admission before the Supreme Court that hospitals routinely overcharge customers for drugs and other products offers a faint hope for a healthier drug-price control regime. But establishing a comprehensive one could be tricky. Western countries that impose limits on drug-pricing margins and manufacturers’ costs — such as Canada or nations of the European Union — do so via near-universal health care programmes that involve bulk (and in that sense monopoly) purchases. India’s health system, on the other hand, is increasingly driven by private-sector delivery, where monitoring price caps is a challenging proposition and largely depends on forbearance on the part of hospitals, clinics and chemists. Nevertheless, the problem is serious enough for the government to consider some level of intervention following the public-interest litigation (PIL), seeking the apex court’s intervention to regulate the prices of generic medicines, drugs and medical equipment. The affidavit had stated that hospital markups on many drugs range between 170 per cent and 700 per cent,  while those on consumables range from 100 per cent to 1,000 per cent. The court itself had described as “dacoity” the markup on the maximum retail price of a range of life-saving drugs, especially cancer drugs. The government has acknowledged that the information asymmetry between patient and hospital is the chief reason for this blatant price gouging. At least part of the problem lies in the government’s drug price-control regime. Medicines are divided into “scheduled” drugs, which are essential medicines that have ceiling prices set by the government — such as insulin, some antibiotics and anti-depressants, tuberculosis medications — and “non-scheduled” drugs, which allow manufacturers to set prices. Over 80 per cent of drugs fall in the non-scheduled category — and that includes cancer drugs. Facing up to this incontrovertible evidence of these pricing practices — that can often tip families into bankruptcy — the government machinery has moved to address the issue. With effect from November 9, 2026, the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) has capped the trade margins on 137 anti-cancer drugs at 30 per cent of the maximum retail price (MRP). The intervention is expected to lower the MRP on life-saving cancer drugs by up to 70 per cent. A parliamentary standing committee has recommended — not for the first time — standardising private-hospital costs, capping room rents to three-star hotel rates, and enforcing mandatory disclosure of upfront costs of medical procedures.  The obvious question is the efficacy with which such diktats can be imposed. Drug-price control runs the risk of being self-defeating. The supply of key molecules for several bulk drugs shifted to China after price controls made them unprofitable for local manufacturers. Today, India imports two-thirds of its active pharmaceutical ingredients from China, the impact of which was keenly felt during the Covid lockdown. Countries with price-control regimes have also felt the impact of manufacturers’ reluctance to introduce the latest drugs into those markets. The government, therefore, needs to navigate between producer and retail profiteering and patients’ interests. Widely disseminated education and a multilingual campaign on patient rights and price policies would go a long way in bridging the information gap. The fact that the NPPA falls under the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilisers rather than the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, which is responsible for health care delivery, suggests a fundamental policy disconnect, which too should be addressed.   Topics : Business Standard Editorial Comment BS Opinion high drug prices cancer treatment health care sector Medicine prices

entry.title: Seamless credit network
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Seamless credit networkSeamless credit network

Interoperability can enable inclusive lending

premium

The RBI's push for interoperability among account aggregators aims to simplify consent-based financial data sharing, improve credit access and reduce loan application dropouts.| Photo: Shutterstock

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 26 2026 | 10:08 PM ISTThe Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) decision to introduce interoperability among account aggregators (AAs) by December 31 seeks to simplify financial-data sharing, which could help reduce loan-application dropoffs. The need for this is underlined by the rapid growth of the AA ecosystem. According to the CRIF Credit Information Services and industry alliance Sahamati, the AA framework facilitated an estimated ₹3.82 trillion in loan disbursements across 36.8 million accounts in 2025-26, accounting for 8.4 per cent of retail lending and loans to micro, small and medium enterprises by value and 11.8 per cent by volume. By September, the ecosystem had fulfilled 595 million consents. More importantly, it is reaching borrowers often overlooked by conventional lending models. In the year ended June 2026, borrowers new to credit accounted for 28.5 per cent of business loans worth ₹10 lakh-25 lakh issued by AA-enabled lenders, against 8.6 per cent for other lenders. In personal loans, their share was 9 per cent, compared with 3.8 per cent through conventional channels. In 2025-26, the value of AA-enabled lending was estimated to be about 1.1 per cent of India’s gross domestic product.  The framework addresses a longstanding problem in the Indian lending ecosystem. Individuals and small businesses without established credit histories often struggle to obtain formal loans even when they have regular incomes or viable businesses. Traditional assessments rely heavily on credit history and require borrowers to submit bank statements, tax documents, and other paperwork. The AA framework allows lenders to access financial information directly from participating institutions, with borrowers’ consent. This enables a more comprehensive assessment of repayment capacity. Its benefits extend beyond loan approvals. The study found that, in lending for two-wheelers, the share of loans overdue by more than 90 days was 0.5 per cent for AA-enabled originations, compared with 5.3 per cent for conventional loans. Greater access, therefore, need not come at the cost of weaker credit quality.  However, differences in technical standards, system reliability, and integration costs could undermine the benefits. Banks, non-banking financial companies, and AA platforms must adopt common protocols, ensure reliable data transfers, and minimise transaction failures. Transparent pricing and clear accountability for failed consent requests or incomplete data sharing will also be necessary. Data protection is equally important. Financial information can reveal sensitive details about an individual’s income, spending and liabilities. Strong encryption, access controls, independent security audits, and effective grievance redress are essential to maintain public trust. It is also important to ensure that smaller lenders are not disadvantaged by high integration costs. Research by the RBI-promoted Centre for Advanced Financial Research and Learning has associated greater exposure to the AA rollout with higher local economic activity. While this does not establish that AAs alone caused the increase, it points to their wider potential. Interoperability can help realise that potential provided efficiency is matched by safeguards. Better data sharing should make credit easier to access without compromising borrowers’ privacy or financial security. With 17 AAs operating in the ecosystem, better connectivity with banks, insurers and pension-related institutions could enable consent-based sharing of a broader range of financial information for inclusion.   Topics : BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Bank credit RBI lending loans Loan pricing

entry.title: Value buying
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Value buyingValue buying

Investors are betting on the transformation of Indian IT

premium

Indian IT companies look to boost growth through artificial intelligence

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 10:24 PM ISTThe Nifty Information-Technology (IT) Index last week hit a 10-month high. The sector index is up over 11 per cent in the past one month, in contrast to the benchmark Nifty 50, which is down 3.6 per cent. One reason is that the first-half results of IT companies have met expectations, and future demand is judged stable, going by admittedly cautious guidance. Another reason for the rally is low valuations. The sector’s average valuations are down to levels that have not been seen since the subprime crisis of 2008. Low PE (price-to-earnings) multiples are attracting value investors, who are betting on valuation rebounds. Going by guidance, demand will not spike. But stable demand should translate into steady, if moderate, growth in constant-currency terms. Given a trend of rupee weakness, the returns may be higher and provide a hedge against currency volatility.  Such cyclical considerations, the key questions for long-term investors, revolve around the Indian IT sector’s ability to leverage the structural changes imposed by artificial intelligence (AI). Trends in software and IT services have decoupled. The AI productivity gains that are expanding software’s pricing potential are also compressing billable hours for services. Enterprises are rejigging budgets to invest in cloud infrastructure and AI-enabled platforms, as evidenced by hyperscaler growth. In the past two years, this divergence has led to a relative de-rating of IT services. But there are signs that India’s IT sector has learnt how to survive and, maybe, thrive, under this new paradigm. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), HCL Tech, Infosys, Tech Mahindra and others have all increased their internal productivity metrics via AI and have started rolling out AI-driven offers for clients. Their management has highlighted opportunities emerging across AI.  Often in partnership with AI-specific players such as OpenAI and Anthropic, Indian IT majors are finding ways to create niches in an ecosystem where every enterprise is looking at AI. Infosys, for example, is helping the banking and financial sector to accelerate AI-driven transformation, using its Topaz offers. HCL Tech has its five-pillar AI strategy and offers like AI Force and HCLTech Pulse. Tech Mahindra has its Zero Gravity Architecture, which helps enterprises prepare for AI deployment. TCS says its AI-revenues contribute over 10 per cent of its top line on an annualised basis. It is also developing a presence in data centres. The amount of demand (in terms of client budgets) is largely unchanged, though the attention has shifted to AI. Spending by the banking, financial services, and insurance (BFSI) sector is concentrated on core modernisation, cloud, data and AI, while technology clients are investing in physical AI. Management commentary indicates that pricing deflation for services may be close to an inflection, since contracts have already undergone repricing over the past two years. One advantage with AI adoption is that the total contract value is realised in shorter timeframes, allowing quicker recognition of revenues and fast pivots in resource deployment. Assuming IT-services firms can partner AI companies to deliver speed, efficiency, and productivity benefits, they could move past the old model of labour arbitrage. Investors buying into IT services during this valuation nadir are betting on this transformation.     Topics : Artificial intelligence Indian IT industry Nifty IT services Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Glitter of gold loans
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Glitter of gold loansGlitter of gold loans

Increasing household debt needs careful examination

premium

Rising gold loans and household debt raise concerns over repayment capacity and financial stability in India

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 10:17 PM ISTA report in this newspaper last week underscored early signs of stress in the rapidly growing gold-loan segment. Although the stress doesn’t pose a systemic risk, the underlying dynamics of this segment and the broader signals need careful examination. In principle, a gold loan is an excellent proposition. Borrowers offer their gold holding as collateral, which gives lenders the confidence to lend even to those who would otherwise not have been able to borrow from the formal sector. Lenders can sell the pledged gold if a borrower is unable to repay the loan. Nevertheless, a large number of defaults can create problems for lenders, depending on gold prices and other terms and conditions.  As the chief executive of a prominent non-banking financial company (NBFC) told this newspaper, between 15 and 23 per cent of the gross gold loans at an aggregate level last financial year went to borrowers who were overdue for more than 90 days on other outstanding loans. This effectively means that nearly one in every four to five borrowers took a gold loan to repay other loans. Thus, the new loan is unlikely to improve the borrower’s ability to repay. This is important from both lenders’ and a macro standpoint. Analysts note that gold loans have become the second-largest retail lending category after home loans. According to the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) data, the outstanding gold loans for banks increased by over 80 per cent, year-on-year, to about ₹5.6 trillion as of August 31. NBFCs have also witnessed sharp increases and have gold-loan books worth about ₹3.6 trillion.  While banks and NBFCs will possibly adjust their lending practices to deal with delinquent borrowers, it appears that some households are becoming more indebted. Notably, household debt in India is growing. The RBI’s last Financial Stability Report (June 2026) showed that household debt at the end of September 2025 was worth 45.5 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP). The level was at 37.6 per cent at the end of March 2023. Although India’s household debt is lower than that of some of the other emerging economies, such as China (59 per cent) and Malaysia (69.9 per cent), it is higher than that of Brazil (36.7 per cent) and South Africa (33.6 per cent), and is increasing. It is worth noting that consumption-related loans are the main driver of household borrowing in India. The share of loans for consumption purposes was at about 50 per cent at the end of March 2026.  Overall, according to the RBI’s assessment, even though household borrowing is rising, the share of higher-rated borrowers has improved. While the aggregate level of household debt may not look high compared with many other countries, the increase in consumption loans needs attention. The share of housing loans in household borrowing is declining. On the contrary, household debt in the United States, for example, is overwhelmingly dominated by housing loans. The increasing household borrowing for consumption could mean that credit is now available more easily and households are frontloading consumption. From the banking and regulation perspective, this may not be a problem, given that asset quality is improving. However, the debt-servicing burden on households could affect overall consumption and growth in the medium term. This could also have repercussions for household savings, with implications for overall investment in the economy. Therefore, the increase in household debt and its composition must be examined carefully.     Topics : Reserve Bank of India gold loans Household debt Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

entry.title: Choices between worthy goals pulling in different directions
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Specials / Choices between worthy goals pulling in different directionsChoices between worthy goals pulling in different directions

Good policy lies in balancing competing priorities, from affordability and innovation to inclusion and protection, while ensuring growth, accountability and long-term sustainability

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Reetesh Anand New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTGood policy is not so much about a choice between right and wrong as it is between two worthwhile goals pulling in different directions. Health care must be affordable, but innovation needs incentives. Credit should be easier to access, but data and borrowers need protection. Domestic investors can support markets, but global competitiveness still matters. Boards must supervise without micromanaging. Businesses can pursue purpose, but they cannot ignore economic viability. The difficulty begins when both objectives are legitimate. Our first editorial today, “Pricing pain points”, looks at health care price controls. The impulse to make treatment more affordable is understandable, especially in a country where out-of-pocket medical spending remains high. But blunt price intervention can create unintended consequences by weakening incentives for companies to launch new medicines, invest in innovation or supply products sustainably. The challenge is to improve affordability without undermining the economics that make better treatment possible. Access matters, but so does the capacity to keep producing what patients need. The second editorial, “Seamless credit network”, looks at interoperable digital lending. Better sharing of financial information can make credit more accessible, particularly for borrowers who are poorly served by traditional banking. But greater connectivity also raises questions about consent, privacy, data security, responsible lending and competition. Inclusion cannot come at the cost of weaker safeguards. A credit network becomes genuinely useful only when convenience and protection advance together. In “Risk of irrelevance?”, Akash Prakash talks about the tension in Indian equities. Domestic investors have supported the market even as foreign investors have sold heavily. That is a source of strength, but it should not become a reason to dismiss prolonged underperformance or declining international interest. India still needs to remain attractive to global capital. A deeper domestic investor base can reduce dependence on foreign flows, but it cannot substitute for earnings growth, competitive valuations and confidence in India’s long-term economic prospects. Rama Bijapurkar’s column, “Uneasy lies the governance space”, examines the boundary between boards and management. Boards are meant to challenge, oversee and protect shareholder interests, but not to run the company. Management needs enough freedom to operate effectively, but it cannot be allowed to escape scrutiny. Trouble begins when oversight turns into interference or autonomy turns into unaccountability. Good governance depends on keeping that boundary clear. M S Sriram’s review of Eric Ries’ Incorruptible, “The double-edged sword of a dual bottom line”, confronts the tension between profit and purpose. Organisations that pursue both commercial returns and social objectives can create powerful models, but they also face competing incentives and difficult accountability questions. The hardest systems, these pieces show, are not those with one goal. They are those with two good ones. Success depends on knowing where the balance lies.
