entry.title: Best of Business Standard Opinion: Resilience comes from widening the base
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Specials / Best of Business Standard Opinion: Resilience comes from widening the baseBest of Business Standard Opinion: Resilience comes from widening the base

Even knowledge systems are stronger when authority is distributed rather than concentrated

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Reetesh Anand3 min read Last Updated : Oct 26 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTYou can’t build resilience by putting everything behind one answer. A household that leans too heavily on gold-backed borrowing becomes vulnerable to asset prices. An investor who treats an entire sector as one trade can miss differences between firms. A country that relies on a single policy tool to manage external stress discovers its limits. Agriculture becomes more fragile when crop diversity narrows. Even knowledge systems are stronger when authority is distributed rather than concentrated. “Glitter of gold loans”, our first editorial today, looks at the rapid growth of household borrowing against gold. Gold is convenient collateral and gives lenders security, which explains why these loans are popular. But the editorial warns that the pace of expansion deserves scrutiny. When household borrowing rises alongside high gold prices, apparent comfort can conceal underlying stress. A strong collateral asset does not eliminate repayment risk, and excessive dependence on gold-backed credit can become a vulnerability if household finances weaken or asset prices reverse.  The second editorial, “Value buying”, looks at Indian IT sector. Artificial intelligence is reshaping this sector, changing client spending and causing company strategies to diverge. That makes blanket sector calls less useful. Investors need to look more closely at productivity, adaptability, valuations, client exposure and each company’s ability to navigate technological change. Indian IT is no longer one homogeneous bet; resilience in investing comes from distinguishing between firms rather than treating the sector as a single trade. In “Ten rules for external sector stress”, Ajay Shah, K P Krishnan and G Padmanabhan make the diversification argument more directly. External shocks cannot be managed through one instrument, whether that is defending the rupee, using reserves or tightening monetary policy. Exchange-rate flexibility, fiscal discipline, banking resilience, capital flows, reserves and institutional credibility all have a role. The lesson from past episodes of stress is to maintain several lines of defence rather than place excessive faith in any one of them. Surinder Sud’s column, “The neglected species of pulses”, brings the theme to agriculture. India’s focus on a relatively small group of major pulses has left many traditional varieties underused. Yet these crops can offer nutritional benefits, suit different agroclimatic conditions and improve resilience to climate stress. A more diverse crop basket can strengthen both food security and farm resilience. “Wikipedia’s origin story, warts and all”, Jennifer Szalai’s review of Richard Cooke’s The Last Best Place on the Internet, turns to knowledge. Wikipedia grew by distributing the creation and correction of information across a vast community rather than concentrating authority among a small editorial elite. That openness created governance problems of its own, but it also made the platform unusually adaptive. Resilience, as we see across all these pieces, comes from widening the base — spreading risk and avoiding dependence on a single answer.

entry.title: Ten rules for external sector stress
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Ten rules for external sector stressTen rules for external sector stress

There is wisdom from history in managing the rupee

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Ajay ShahK P KrishnanG Padmanabhan6 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 10:37 PM ISTThere is considerable stress in the Indian external sector. Policymakers see information that we, as external persons, do not. From the outside, it is not useful to comment on the minutiae of tactical policy moves. Drawing on the experiences of crises in the Indian external sector over the past 25 years, we offer 10 principles that are universally useful in understanding the present situation and responding to it.  1. Supply stability, not shocks. Policymakers must be a supplier of stability, not the originator — whether intended or otherwise — of shocks. We should plan every action of policymakers to be calm, reassuring, and predictable. The dharma of modern central banking is “say what you will do and then do what you just said”. Surprises should emanate from the external world — such as the October 14 Houthi attack upon Saudi Aramco in Dhahran — not from the authorities.  2. Leave price discovery to private persons. Speculating about financial prices is the work of private persons, not the Indian state. There will always be legitimate disagreement about what values of the rupee will be, and state agencies should not be put in a position of having to take a stand on this. Getting into dogfights with speculators is problematic. Speculators are a formidable force. Tangling with them is daunting. In addition, policymakers lose strategic sense when they are enveloped in a fog of war. They should be above the fray of the practical details of what is happening in the market: The buying, the selling, and the price.  3. Respect the scale of cross-border flows. The Indian economy is very big, and the money moving across the border is now vast. In 2025-26, gross flows on the current account were $2.18 trillion, while gross private flows on the capital and financial account were $3.21 trillion. Thus, over $5.39 trillion comes in and goes out of India every year. Every dollar out of this is in the command of self-interested and intelligent people who are watching the landscape and trying to earn a profit from currency speculation when opportunities present themselves. When currency speculation through financial instruments becomes difficult, this activity goes into the behaviour of foreign direct investment (FDI), imports, exports, and remittances. The adjustment that is prevented on the exchange rate is concentrated in domestic asset prices.  4. Financial development has hysteresis. It cannot be turned off and on like a tap. A good financial system is ultimately about the emergence of capable teams in Indian and foreign financial firms. Those draw upon decades of investment and sustained knowledge building. When a market’s or a product’s life ends, we lose decades of culture. The threat of future bans lurks in the mind of decision-makers in private financial firms. They respond by investing less in organisational capabilities. This results in a less knowledgeable and less capable financial sector. This is harmful for India. It creates conditions of excess volatility in illiquid financial markets.  5. Get on to the virtuous cycle. Good countries get on to the virtuous cycle of high financial development, high market liquidity, and reduced volatility. However, there can also be the opposite feedback loop: Government management of a price leads to damaged financial development, market illiquidity, greater volatility, and then pressure upon the government to intervene in prices.  6. Treat cross-border friction in a unified way. Indian economic growth is made in the most productive firms, and the most productive firms are the internationalised ones. A firm does not experience each regulatory obstacle in isolation; rules across trade, capital, data, and payments interact as one connected system that shapes how investors judge Indian governance. When greater cross-border friction comes about — against the movement of money across the border, against currency trading, against currency-risk management, against internationalised business activities — these are harmful for Indian economic growth. When we make capital flows and risk management more difficult, this harms stock prices and the exchange rate, as the foreigner demands a higher risk premium.  7. Avoid currency dominance. Every currency defence turns into an interest-rate defence. This induces a loss of autonomy in monetary policy. For decades, Indian economic policy worked to protect monetary policy from “fiscal dominance”, where the short-term interest rate was controlled by the fiscal deficit. We should not now relapse into “currency dominance”. The short-term interest rate should be shaped by inflation forecasts alone, and not get distorted by currency considerations. The 91-day bill went up by about 50 basis points in a month; we should ask whether this conduct was optimal from the viewpoint of the 4 per cent inflation target.  8. Intellectual power beats coercive power. Policymakers are judged every day by the market for the internal consistency and feasibility of their efforts, and for their intellectual capabilities. Policymaking viewed as a power game works poorly as, ultimately, the global financial system is more powerful than the Indian policymaker. The soft power of respect in the eyes of the people who shape business and finance strategy worldwide matters more.  9. Renew vows to the reform strategy. There is only one configuration that is consistent with Indian success: Inflation targeting, a floating exchange rate, and an open capital account. Policymakers need to renew their vows to this strategic picture of Indian economic reforms every few weeks. Reversals of reforms are generally avoidable, they should be accompanied by an apology, and they should concern minor things.  10. Emulate the good countries. There are countries that are basket cases, like Russia or Turkey. India should aim to be like the good ones, like South Korea, Taiwan or Israel, which maintain low cross-border friction across trade, capital, technology, data, and finance. We need to self-consciously up our game and match their policy frameworks, their everyday stream of policy decisions and communication, and their body language.
The writers are, respectively, a researcher at XKDR Forum; an honorary senior fellow at the Isaac Centre for Public Policy, and a former civil servant; and former executive director, Reserve Bank of India     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: From PCA to Prem Watsa: IDBI Bank's long road to privatisation
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / From PCA to Prem Watsa: IDBI Bank's long road to privatisationFrom PCA to Prem Watsa: IDBI Bank's long road to privatisation

Banks in a growing economy need patient, long-term foreign capital with good governance to meet credit demand

premium

For IDBI Bank, the February 2021 Budget announced the government's plan for strategic disinvestment; an in-principle Cabinet approval followed in May 2021 (Photo: Bloomberg)

Tamal Bandyopadhyay7 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 9:53 PM ISTWhat do IDBI Bank Ltd and Air India have in common? For both, privatisation turned into a five-year plan. Of course, the erstwhile Planning Commission is not involved in their cases!  Following Cabinet approval in June 2017, the government invited expressions of interest (EoIs) for Air India in March 2018, offering a 76 per cent stake, but it drew no bids. A revised plan offering 100 per cent was launched in January 2020; the Tata Group won the bid in October 2021 and took over the airline in January 2022.  For IDBI Bank, the February 2021 Budget announced the government's plan for strategic disinvestment; an in-principle Cabinet approval followed in May 2021. EoIs were invited in October 2022.  In March 2023, the then Department of Investment and Public Asset Management Secretary Tuhin Kanta Pandey (now chairman of the capital market regulator) tweeted: "Reports appearing in a section of the media indicating the possibility of deferment of IDBI Bank disinvestment are misleading… The transaction continues to be on track as per the defined process in the post-EoI stage following receipts of multiple EoIs."  In March 2026, the government called off the first round after financial bids from Fairfax Financial Holdings Ltd and Emirates NBD fell short of the reserve price. Revised bids came in by July 2026.  On October 14, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs approved Canada's Fairfax as the strategic buyer. Fairfax will buy the 60.72 per cent stake (30.48 per cent from the government and 30.24 per cent from Life Insurance Corporation of India, or LIC) for ₹52,878 crore. This will be the largest foreign direct investment in the history of India's financial sector. The deal is expected to close by March 2027, once all approvals are in place.  Fairfax plans to bring IDBI Bank, Go Digit Insurance, and IIFL Capital Services Ltd under one umbrella, creating a large integrated financial group on Indian turf. Fairfax is the controlling promoter of Go Digit General Insurance Ltd. Its stake in IIFL Capital is 30.2 per cent, and it is in the process of raising it to 51 per cent.  It also holds 40 per cent in CSB Bank Ltd. We don't know where CSB Bank fits into Fairfax's scheme of things. It may merge it with IDBI Bank or sell its stake to another investor. It has a two-year window to resolve the overlap.  Indeed, the IDBI Bank privatisation took a long time, but it is yet another signal of how the approach of the government and the banking regulator to the financial sector is changing.  Once upon a time, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) was looking for a suitor for United Western Bank Ltd. Standard Chartered Bank was among 17 contenders, but an acquisition by a foreign bank was a big no-no in the RBI's playbook in those days. In 2006, the Satara-based old private bank was merged with IDBI Bank.  Before that, HSBC had acquired a 20 per cent stake in UTI Bank Ltd (now Axis Bank Ltd) in December 2003. Under the RBI's ownership norms, it had to pare its stake to below 5 per cent in 2006, and it eventually exited in 2012, nearly a decade after the acquisition.  Things started changing in the middle of the last decade. In December 2016, the RBI allowed Fairfax to take a majority stake in Catholic Syrian Bank Ltd, the first time a foreign investor had been permitted to control an Indian bank. Fairfax recapitalised it, renamed it CSB Bank, and listed it on the bourses in 2019.  Japan's Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC) holds 24.99 per cent in Yes Bank Ltd. Dubai-based Emirates NBD completed the acquisition of a 60 per cent controlling stake in RBL Bank Ltd in June 2026.  Among other large single investors, Warburg Pincus has close to 10 per cent of IDFC First Bank Ltd, and Blackstone will have 9.99 per cent of Federal Bank Ltd once its warrants are converted.  The RBI has progressively raised the voting-rights ceiling for a single shareholder in a private bank from 10 per cent to 26 per cent, and case-by-case exemptions on ownership are made, depending on the circumstances. CSB Bank was the first experiment with such an exemption, and a successful one.  The reasons behind the exemptions differ: Stress at a bank, a strategic goal of building a larger entity, or the government wanting to encash value. In the case of IDBI Bank, the government will get about ₹26,543 crore for its 30.48 per cent. It can make more later, as it will still hold 15 per cent in the bank.  Banks in a growing economy need patient, long-term foreign capital with good governance to meet credit demand. The direction is right.  Overall foreign direct investment (FDI) in private banks is permitted up to 74 per cent – 49 per cent through the automatic route, and investment between 49 and 74 per cent needing government approval. For public sector banks, the FDI ceiling is 20 per cent and government ownership cannot fall below 51 per cent.  It has been a different Diwali for both IDBI Bank and its MD and CEO Rakesh Sharma. He took charge in October 2018, a few weeks before that year's Diwali; eight years on, the strategic sale has come just ahead of another Diwali. Sharma, whose current tenure runs till March 2028, will remain at the helm.  It has not been an easy task.  The RBI placed IDBI Bank under the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework in May 2017 because of its high net non-performing assets (NPAs) and negative return on assets. PCA restricted the bank's lending, branch expansion, and hiring.  Nearly one-third of the bank's loan portfolio had turned bad. By September 2018, its gross NPAs were 31.78 per cent, the highest bad-loan ratio ever recorded by an Indian commercial bank. In that quarter, net NPAs were 17.3 per cent, a tad lower than 18.76 per cent in June.  IDBI Bank also holds the record for losses – for 13 successive quarters, between December 2016 and December 2019. During this period, it accumulated net losses of about ₹41,800 crore, driven by massive provisioning for its ballooning NPAs.  Following capital infusions from the government and ₹21,624 crore from LIC, which took a 51 per cent controlling stake in January 2019, the RBI reclassified it as a private sector bank. The bank broke its losing streak in the March 2020 quarter with a net profit of ₹135 crore, and a year later, in March 2021, the PCA restrictions were lifted. After a gap of eight years, it paid a dividend (10 per cent) for FY2023.  Since returning to profit in March 2020, IDBI Bank has not looked back. In the September 2026 quarter, its gross NPAs were 2.12 per cent and net NPAs 0.17 per cent. It made a net profit of ₹2,205 crore in the quarter and ₹4,320 crore in the first half of the current fiscal. Its net interest margin was 4.11 per cent in September, 0.50 percentage point higher than in June.  One contributing factor has been cutting down high-cost bulk deposits.   Meanwhile, the once-corporate lender is now a retail bank, with retail loans accounting for nearly 70 per cent of its ₹2.72 trillion loan book. Finally, its capital adequacy ratio is 27.1 per cent, which means it can grow substantially without raising fresh capital. What else does a bank need?   ____________________________________________________________________________________________________  The writer is an author and senior advisor to Jana Small Finance Bank Ltd. entry.title: Refining the crude argument
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Refining the crude argumentRefining the crude argument

Anti-Americanism is chronic, deep-rooted, and instinctive in India, cutting across party lines. We only undermine our own interests by doing so

premium

Reliance's Jamnagar refinery has emerged as a strategic asset in India's energy sector, strengthening the country's position in global crude oil processing and fuel exports. | Image : PTI

Shekhar Gupta7 min read Last Updated : Oct 24 2026 | 9:30 AM ISTHumble Jamnagar dominated headlines and airtime this week. The visit by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Ambassador Sergio Gor to the Reliance refinery township painted on the political radar screen and stood out in domestic debate.  That they were hosted by the Ambanis became a key talking point. Why are the Americans taking such interest in Indian refining? Why are they asking the Ambanis to buy Venezuelan oil? Why are they calling India a refining superpower and asking us to increase capacities? Or to sum up, why were Rubio and Gor in Jamnagar and not in Delhi or Bengaluru, as visiting dignitaries did in the past?  Go back to the United Progressive Alliance era. There was zero controversy over Western heads of state being shown around the Infosys or other tech campuses. The reaction was unanimous: national pride. This also cut across political divides. Even the Left put its anti-corporate instincts aside.  Why, then, are we now seeing such suspicion, scepticism, even paranoia? Why are the Ambanis (and India) being forced to buy oil from the most distant point possible (Venezuela) when Russia is so much closer? Of course, it must be arm-twisting to sell Venezuelan oil the Americans control, and a ploy to wean us away from Russia to squeeze Putin.  None of this passes the most cursory fact-check, but why let that confuse you out of a delicious outrage.  India’s crude purchases from Russia haven’t dramatically declined and are unlikely to. To call India a refining superpower isn’t just a great compliment, but it reminds us of a marvellous new element in our Comprehensive National Power (CNP). The late Dhirubhai Ambani’s foresight has given his nation a workaround for the curse of not having energy resources.  What does a nation of our size do when it is blessed with almost no hydrocarbons? It starts refining at a global scale what others pump out of their soil or seabed. Without refining, crude is nothing. Global refining capacities were not keeping pace with the rising energy consumption. India filled in that gap. The Ambanis’ foresight also lies in recognising the peculiar Venezuelan heavy-crude challenge, and opportunity.  If this made India a refining superpower, isn’t that something to be as proud of as tech and outsourcing in Bengaluru? Let’s understand some realities. Today, the American need for global refining capacities, especially for the waxy Venezuelan crude is strategic, political and economic — in that order.  Strategic, because the Americans have just forced regime change in Venezuela, which holds the largest crude reserves in the world. They have to consummate their success commercially as they set about redesigning the Western hemisphere to align with their interests. India has no dog in that fight.  Politically, more crude oil in global markets moderates prices. The Iran situation isn’t settling down. If anything, it might get worse after the US midterms.  Economically, the US gets a commercial take, or cut, from Venezuelan oil sales. And the more refined products enter global markets, the more fuel prices in the US decline. It may be too late for the midterms now. But in the American system, jockeying for the next presidential election begins just after the midterms, especially if the incumbent is finishing the second term. The Republicans, not exactly topping the charts at this point, want inflation, and gasoline prices to go down.  This needs more crude oil, and more refining. America is still among the largest importers of Venezuelan oil. But over the past decades, many of its heavy-crude refineries shut down as its economy moved to the softer, wealthier and less resource-dependent avenues: Tech, finance, rocketry and now artificial intelligence (AI). Generally, you can say, as Texas, Detroit and the rust belt have yielded to Silicon Valley, Seattle and New York.  In this situation, which country can play refiner to the world but India? Europe has minimal refining capacity that survived its Greta Thunbergs. West Asia wouldn’t dare expand while there’s the Iranian threat and its proxies stalk the peninsula with ballistic missiles and drones.  It’s been said often that if Bengaluru were to suffer a catastrophic power or internet outage, a lot of the world would come to a standstill. If that’s leverage, an element in our CNP, why shouldn’t refining be so? India should, if anything, add more refineries and at scale. Even Reliance should build another Jamnagar, preferably along the eastern seaboard. Some of these could be built in conjunction with small modular reactors (SMRs).  The fears come from all sides. The Left, you’d expect. But also the Right and the Centre. That is, if you could describe today’s Congress as centrist, though I’d think their current Left tilt is for product-differentiation rather than a de-canonisation of Manmohan Singh.  The Right is also bemused. Why America? And why the Ambanis? It doesn’t matter to them that Rubio also met N Chandrasekaran of Tata Sons and Gautam Adani. Because then, why only the oligarchs?  Broadly, all are jolted because of the twin factor of America and Ambani. Anti-Americanism is chronic, deep and instinctive in India. If America suggests you do something, or says thank you for doing it, be very afraid. Hide. There must be a terrifying hidden motive. This cuts across party-lines, and the BJP or its base isn’t immune either. Add to this that oldest Indian fear, even contempt for the “evil corporate”.  In the Nehru-Indira era “Birla-Tata” was a cuss word. Now it’s “Ambani-Adani”. After all, that’s what the socialist brainwashing from our politics, literature and movies scarred us with. The standout line that conditioned generations comes from Dilip Kumar in the 1957 Naya Daur, speaking on behalf of labour: “Jhagda toh haath aur machine ka hai (it’s a tussle between human labour and machinery).” The capitalist has rarely been portrayed as even a half-decent character in our popular culture.  Flip the card. Aren’t we so happy when our Prime Ministers, or even chief ministers, visit the US, Japan, or France with key industrial plants and tech campuses on their itinerary? Or when Prime Minister Narendra Modi goes to meet Mark Zuckerberg at Menlo Park, invites Elon Musk, kids and all, for a private meeting and generously meets visiting CEOs?  As for the Congress, they should remember how Rajiv Gandhi brought the tech revolution to India. On his first visit to the US in June 1985, he reached out to Mark Shepherd Jr of Texas Instruments and persuaded him to set up his offshore unit in Bengaluru. Subsequently, he met Jack Welch of GE. Welch was told if he wanted India to buy his engines, he must buy software from our companies. Wipro and GE set up a joint venture. Some detail on how GE was wooed by Sam Pitroda, Montek Singh Ahluwalia and Jairam Ramesh is found in DLF founder K P Singh’s sequel memoir Why the Heck Not?  We undermine our national interest first, by not shedding our permanent anti-Americanism, still rooted in 1971. And second, by dismissing our entrepreneurs as exploiters, not builders of India.  The first needs to be seen in the perspective of the day. Nations relate to each other after weighing self-interest, and not protocol. In any case, what’s protocol in Trump’s times? And a society that doesn’t respect its own entrepreneurial successes is condemned to falling behind.  The only thing wrong with the fact that India has the Ambanis, Tatas, Adanis, Birlas, Jindals and Mittals is that there are so few of them. India needs some more. Let them build more refineries, steel plants, smelt copper and aluminium for the world, write software, build global capability centres, set up power plants. India has to learn to celebrate its entrepreneurs. Jamnagar is only a symbol and reminder of what India can become.
